A common idea is telephony by neural implant--the equivalent of a smartphone as an implantable chip or set of chips that will provide one with a kind of personal HUD and visual AR projection system linked to the optic nerve and a virtual audio interface. This would also afford VR capability as the tech develops to allow more sensory channels to be intercepted or bypassed to receive virtual input.

But we don't actually need that advanced a technology to implement some of this capability. There's a technique called sub-vocal speech recognition that allows a computer to detect, through the surface of the skin, the unconscious myoelectric signals generated in the larynx when we think about speaking but don't actually speak--subvocalization. This is why some people have that habit of mimicking what people say to them in a whisper or whisper when they're reading or typing. Those subvocal signals are just a little bit stronger for them than the average person. NASA explored development of this technology as a means of giving astronauts a way to communicate silently with computers while wearing a spacesuit. They could think command words to them and those thoughts would be detected as subvocal signals. More recently this has been demonstrated as a means of two-way communication by combining it with text-to-speech. A computer detects your subvocal speech, translates it to ASCII, transmits that over the internet, then the receiving computer converts that from text-to-speech in a simulation of the sender's voice. Done in both directions, one can conduct a conversation entirely by thinking rather than actually speaking, and all that is needed is a soft collar with some sensors. No brain surgery required.

So I suspect a kind of smartphone based on something like a Bluetooth headset and soft collar may soon appear, first as a peripheral for existing smartphones and then a whole self-contained phone based on the use of an all-audio user interface driven by subvocal speech command. This may also evolve into an alternative to keyboards without the downsides of earlier speech recognition software, which was never discreet enough to be practical for real work in an office setting.

But it's tricky. Mobile communications has often evolved in ways that didn't seem to make much sense to me. People seem oblivious to the potential of devices to make them look asinine or be a nuisance to those around them. For instance, I always anticipated a device like the typical smartphone would become commonplace, but as a pocket PAD, not as a phone. It never made sense to me that people would commonly put a touchscreen up against their face. It's a little gross when you think about it... And the screens just don't work well in an outdoor environment. When I was younger, we expected the mobile phone to evolve into something minimal, sleek, durable, and jewelry-like rather than some kind of bulky digital Swiss Army Knife. Something in a form like the Samsung SlimStick or the Elecom Pen bluetooth handsets that can conveniently fit in a shirt pocket and which would be controlled entirely by speech. If you have capability like Siri or Cortana, you don't need a screen--at least for the simple tasks of operating a phone. It seems bizarre to me that we still talk about 'phone companies' at all.
